pentestTypes.title: Types of pentest
pentestTypes.intro: How much you hand over at the start decides how far a test can go. All three are run by our own pentesters, working with an AI agent set up for that level of access.

black.name: Black box
black.summary: We start with nothing but your address, exactly as a real attacker would. The most realistic test, and usually the shortest list of findings.

grey.name: Grey box
grey.summary: You give us a login, so we can test everything your own users can reach. That usually finds considerably more.

white.name: White box
white.summary: You give us the source code as well. Nothing stays hidden, and the report points at the exact lines to fix.

definition.title: What web application pentesting is
definition.p1: Web application pentesting is a security assessment in which your application is attacked under controlled conditions, exactly as a real attacker would, but ending in a report instead of an incident. Everything a user can reach is in scope: the login, the roles behind it, the data each account can touch and the business logic tying it all together.
definition.p2: We combine experienced European pentesters with AI-supported security tooling. The agents cover the breadth of the application while our specialists chase the findings that need human judgment.

coverage.title: What we test
coverage.intro: We test with autonomous AI agents, following the OWASP Top 10 and PTES.

auth.title: Authentication and sessions
auth.body: Login flows, multi-factor authentication, password reset, session handling and how long a token stays valid.

accessControl.title: Authorization and access control
accessControl.body: Broken access control, IDOR, privilege escalation and whether one customer can reach another customer's data.

injection.title: Injection and input handling
injection.body: SQL injection, cross-site scripting, template and command injection, and everything else that follows unvalidated input.

businessLogic.title: Business logic
businessLogic.body: Order flows, pricing, quotas and approval steps, abused in ways an automated scanner never finds.

configuration.title: Configuration and hardening
configuration.body: Security headers, TLS, exposed admin interfaces, verbose error messages and outdated components.

dataExposure.title: Data exposure
dataExposure.body: Personal data reachable without authorization, API responses that give away too much, and information disclosure with GDPR impact.

process.title: How a pentest runs

blackbox.q: What is the difference between blackbox and greybox testing?
blackbox.a: In a blackbox test we start with nothing more than a URL, exactly like an outside attacker. In a greybox test you give us accounts and, if you want, documentation or source access, so we reach the deeper layers of the application within the same amount of time. Most organizations get more out of greybox.

duration.q: How long does a pentest take?
duration.a: That depends on the size of your application and the number of roles in it. We determine the effort during scoping and put it in writing before we start, so the scope and the price are agreed up front.

production.q: Can you test our production environment?
production.a: Yes, and we regularly do. We agree a test window in advance and treat destructive actions as out of scope unless you explicitly ask for them. If you would rather we work on an acceptance environment, that works too.

remediation.q: Do you help fix the findings as well?
remediation.a: You get concrete recommendations for every finding, and we are happy to walk your developers through them. Once a fix is live we retest it, so you know it holds.

compliance.q: Does a pentest help with ISO 27001 or NIS2?
compliance.a: A pentest gives you demonstrable evidence for a certification or audit track. Through ARGUS every finding is mapped to the relevant ISO 27001 controls, which makes reporting on your security posture considerably simpler.

definition.title: What API pentesting is
definition.p1: API pentesting is a security assessment of the interface itself, rather than of anything drawn on top of it. Every endpoint, parameter, token and role is attacked under controlled conditions, including the calls your own front end never makes. That is exactly where an attacker starts.
definition.p2: We combine experienced European pentesters with AI-supported tooling. The agents work through the surface at scale, every endpoint against every role, while our specialists chase the flaws that need a person to understand what the calls are for.

coverage.title: What we test
coverage.intro: REST, GraphQL, gRPC and the SOAP services still quietly holding a business together. Every endpoint, against every role.

auth.title: Authentication and tokens
auth.body: JWT handling and signature validation, OAuth flows, API keys, refresh logic and how long a stolen token stays useful.

authorization.title: Authorization per object
authorization.body: Broken object-level authorization, function-level gaps, role escalation and whether one tenant's identifier reaches another tenant's data.

dataExposure.title: What comes back
dataExposure.body: Responses returning more than the screen shows, mass assignment on the way in, and errors that describe your internals with GDPR impact attached.

rateLimits.title: Rate limits and abuse
rateLimits.body: Throttling, quotas and lockout, plus the endpoints an attacker can turn into an expense: enumeration, brute force and costly queries.

businessLogic.title: Business logic
businessLogic.body: Order, payment and approval calls made out of sequence, replayed, or carrying values no client of yours would ever send.

configuration.title: Configuration and transport
configuration.body: CORS, TLS, HTTP methods, verbose errors, debug routes and old API versions still answering after the new one shipped.

process.title: How an API test runs
process.intro: Six stages, from the first call to the retest. At every point you know what is happening and what comes next.

protocols.q: Which kinds of API do you test?
protocols.a: REST and GraphQL most often, and gRPC, WebSocket and SOAP services just as readily. What matters is not the protocol but whether we can reach it and know which roles are supposed to reach what.

documentation.q: Do you need our OpenAPI specification?
documentation.a: It helps and we will ask for it, along with a Postman collection if you have one. Both let us start on the logic instead of on discovery. Neither is required: we can map the surface from traffic and from the API's own answers, and finding endpoints your specification forgot is often a result in itself.

access.q: What do you need from us?
access.a: Accounts for each role, ideally two per role so we can test whether one account reaches the other's data, plus a reachable environment and a contact who can answer a question during the test.

production.q: Can you test our production API?
production.a: Yes, and we regularly do. We agree a test window in advance and treat destructive actions as out of scope unless you explicitly ask for them. If rate limits or noisy monitoring are a concern we work around them, or you point us at an acceptance environment instead.

compliance.q: Does a pentest help with ISO 27001 or NIS2?
compliance.a: A pentest gives you demonstrable evidence for a certification or audit track. Through ARGUS every finding is mapped to the relevant ISO 27001 controls, which makes reporting on your security posture considerably simpler.

format.q: Is the training on site or online?
format.a: Either, and often both: a live session on site for the discussion, and shorter remote sessions for the people who could not be there or who joined later. What we avoid is a video everybody clicks through in silence.

language.q: In which language do you train?
language.a: Dutch or English, and we will say plainly if a mixed group is better served by one over the other. The material follows the language of the session.

consent.q: May you send our staff phishing without telling them?
consent.a: A simulation only works unannounced, but it is never a secret operation: it is agreed with you in advance, and where a works council or a data protection officer has a say, that conversation happens before anything is sent. Results are reported per group rather than per person. The point is to teach, not to build a list of names.

duration.q: How long does a programme take?
duration.a: A first session is usually half a day. Real change comes from repetition, so a programme normally runs across a year with a small number of moments in it. We put the shape in writing before we start.

measure.q: How do you show it worked?
measure.a: By comparing the same measurements over time: how many people click, how many report, and how quickly. Reporting speed is the number that matters most, and the one that moves first.

definition.title: What security awareness training is
definition.p1: Security awareness training is a programme that changes how your people handle the moments an attacker is counting on: a message that arrives at exactly the right time, a caller who knows just enough, a password that has been reused once too often. It is built around your organisation rather than taken off a shelf, and it runs on a rhythm instead of once a year.
definition.p2: A firewall has never once clicked a link. The people who keep your business running are asked to, dozens of times a week, by messages built to look exactly like the ones they are waiting for.

coverage.title: What a programme covers
coverage.intro: Six subjects, taught with your own tools and your own scenarios rather than stock examples from a slide deck.

phishing.title: Phishing
phishing.body: What a convincing message looks like now that they are written well, arrive on the right day and refer to a project your colleague is genuinely working on, and what to do in the ten seconds after clicking.

socialEngineering.title: Social engineering
socialEngineering.body: The phone call from the supplier, the visitor who follows someone through the door, the urgent request from a director who is conveniently unreachable. Pressure and authority are the tools; recognising them is the training.

passwords.title: Passwords and access
passwords.body: Why reuse is the risk rather than complexity, how a password manager changes the habit, and what multi-factor authentication does and does not protect against.

workingSafely.title: Working safely, day to day
workingSafely.body: Public networks, personal devices, the AI tool nobody registered, and what leaves the building in a shared link or an attachment sent to the wrong autocomplete.

dataLeaks.title: When something goes wrong
dataLeaks.body: How to recognise an incident, who to tell within the hour, and why reporting quickly matters more than not having made the mistake. Blame is what keeps incidents hidden.

reporting.title: Speaking up in time
reporting.body: What counts as suspicious, who to tell, and why saying something an hour after a mistake is worth far more than saying nothing at all.

process.title: How a programme runs
process.intro: A loop, not a course. One session teaches; a rhythm changes what people do.

baseline.title: Measure
baseline.body: We start with where you actually stand, using a simulation and a short survey, so the training answers your situation and you have something to compare against later.

training.title: Train
training.body: Live sessions, on site or remote, in groups small enough that people ask the questions they would otherwise be embarrassed to ask.

simulation.title: Simulate
simulation.body: Realistic phishing sent to your own people, in your own house style, and used to teach at the moment of clicking rather than to catch anyone out.

adjust.title: Adjust
adjust.body: You get the results per department and per scenario, we agree what needs more attention, and the loop starts again where the risk actually is.

comparison.title: Where AssistSec makes the difference
comparison.intro: Awareness is a habit, not a module. That is the whole difference between a programme that changes what people do and one that produces an attendance list.

aboutPage.heroBody: We believe a pentest should not be a yearly ritual. Our pentesters and our AI agents keep testing every month, and you watch the results live instead of waiting for a report.

story.title: Our story
story.p1: AssistSec was started by pentesters who grew annoyed with their own trade. A week of testing, a thick report, a signature and see you next year. Meanwhile the code changes every day, and attackers do not wait for the next audit round.
story.p2: So we built it differently. Our agents keep testing the way we would ourselves, only they never sleep. Everything they find passes a senior pentester before it reaches you. Machines bring the speed, people make the call.

argusWhy.title: Why we built ARGUS
argusWhy.body: A report starts ageing the day it is delivered. ARGUS does not. The portal scans again every month, orders findings by risk, retests the moment you ship a fix and keeps track of where you stand for ISO 27001. You still receive a full pentest report, written to the standard your auditor and your customers expect. What changes is that the report is no longer the only place your security lives: instead of loose PDFs scattered across mailboxes, everything stays current in one place.

manifesto.title: What drives us
manifesto.body: We do not believe in yearly snapshots. Security is a living practice: test continuously, validate every finding with human judgment and stay until it is fixed. That is what drives us.

cta.title: Find your weaknesses before someone else does.
cta.body: Create an ARGUS account and schedule your first pentest in minutes. Findings appear live and the pentesters are one chat away.

hero.body: We combine the most experienced pentesters from Europe with AI-assisted testing to strengthen the security of web applications and APIs. Every finding is validated by an expert, giving organizations clear, reliable insights to fix vulnerabilities before attackers can exploit them.

progress.title: Running your scan

low.title: Nothing notable on the public surface
low.body: This scan found no confirmed issues on the parts of your site that are visible without logging in. That is a good sign, and it is not the same as being secure: most serious findings live behind authentication, where automated checks cannot reach.

moderate.title: Some housekeeping to do
moderate.body: We found configuration gaps that are worth closing. None of them hands an attacker access on their own, but together they make other attacks easier and cheaper.

elevated.title: Issues worth acting on
elevated.body: We confirmed findings that meaningfully weaken your public position. These are the kind of gaps that get used as a stepping stone, and they are usually quick to fix once identified.

high.title: Act on these findings
high.body: We confirmed several significant issues on your public surface. We would recommend addressing them soon and testing the authenticated parts of the application as well.

low.title: No exposure found in the sources we check
low.body: This address did not appear in the breach sources available to us. That is not proof it has never been exposed, only that we found nothing.

moderate.title: This address appears in known breaches
moderate.body_one: We found this address in {{count}} known source. No password exposure was recorded.
moderate.body_other: We found this address in {{count}} known sources. No password exposure was recorded.

elevated.body_one: We found this address in {{count}} known source, including at least one where a password was exposed.
elevated.body_other: We found this address in {{count}} known sources, including at least one where a password was exposed.

high.title: Act on this now
high.body_one: We found this address in {{count}} known source with serious exposure, such as repeated password compromise or malware-harvested credentials.
high.body_other: We found this address in {{count}} known sources with serious exposure, such as repeated password compromise or malware-harvested credentials.

report.emailEmptyBody: This address did not appear in any of the breach sources available to us. New breaches surface regularly, so this reflects what is known today rather than a permanent answer.
report.emptyBody: We could not find issues on the parts of your site reachable without logging in. This is not a clean bill of health: an automated scan cannot reach authorization, business logic or anything behind a login, and those are where the findings that matter usually are.
report.findingsHint: Most serious first. Select one to read the reasoning.

report.lookalikesBody_other: We generated the misspellings and alternative suffixes an attacker would try, and {{count}} of them are registered. Some will be your own defensive registrations.

report.lookalikesMail_other: {{count}} of these can send and receive mail, which is the shape of invoice fraud rather than parked names. Confirm they are yours.

report.stackTitle: What the site is built on
report.title: Your website scan

confirmed.label: Confirmed.
confirmed.body: We observed this directly in the response.

high.label: High confidence.
high.body: Strong indirect evidence. The specific detail may vary.

possible.label: Unverified.
possible.body: This may be a false positive. A person should confirm it before you act on it, and we have not treated it as a finding when calculating your risk band.

limits.known_sources_only: This report covers breach sources available to us today. Absence of a record is not proof an address was never exposed, and new breaches are published regularly.
limits.dnssec_undetermined: We could not reach a validating resolver, so DNSSEC status is unknown for this scan.
limits.no_ct_records: No certificates for this domain appeared in Certificate Transparency logs, so no subdomains were discovered this way.
limits.waf_undetermined: A web application firewall that does not announce itself in its headers would not have been detected. We do not send attack traffic to find one.
limits.unauthenticated_only: Everything here was observed from outside, without an account. What sits behind a login — user data, admin screens, paid features — was not looked at, and that is usually where the impactful findings are.
limits.no_business_logic: This is an automated surface check. It does not try to misuse the application: skipping payment steps, reading another customer's records, or chaining small issues into a large one takes a person, and is what a penetration test is for.
limits.point_in_time: The picture is as of the moment the scan ran. A new subdomain, a certificate reissued tomorrow, or a header change on the next deploy would not be reflected here.

failed.title: The scan could not be completed
failed.body: Something went wrong before we finished. This does not mean nothing was found, only that we could not look properly.

rate_limited.title: Too many requests
rate_limited.body: This connection has started several scans recently. Please wait a few minutes before trying again.

expired.title: This report has expired
expired.body: Reports are deleted after a short retention period. Run a new scan to get a current view.

failureCodes.provider_unavailable: Our data source did not answer. This is a problem on our side, not with your domain.
failureCodes.provider_timeout: The scan took longer than allowed and was stopped. Please try again.
failureCodes.target_blocked: That domain resolves to an address we do not scan, such as a private or internal network.
failureCodes.target_unresolvable: That domain did not resolve. Check the spelling and whether it is publicly reachable.
failureCodes.internal: Something went wrong on our side. Please try again.

actions.passwords: Change the password on any account that used this address, starting with the sources listed above. Do not reuse a password across services.
actions.mfa: Turn on multi-factor authentication wherever it is offered. It is the single most effective step against an exposed password.
actions.monitor: Treat unexpected password reset emails as a warning sign rather than noise, and report them.

graph.title: Digital footprint relationship map
graph.intro: How the exposure connects. Select any point to see where the observation came from, how confident we are, and what to do about it.
graph.subject: Your address
graph.stealerAction: This source is malware-harvested credential data. Treat every account used on the affected device as compromised and change those passwords from a clean device.
graph.passwordAction: Change this password everywhere it was used and enable multi-factor authentication.

explain.subject: The address this report was produced for. It is not displayed here, and it was not included in the email that brought you to this page.
explain.source: A service whose breached data includes this address. The name is as published by the source.
explain.stealer: Credential data harvested by malware from an infected device. This is more serious than a service breach, because it usually captures many accounts at once.
explain.password: A password associated with this address was exposed in this source. We never store, display or handle the password itself in any form.
explain.phone: A phone number appeared in this record. Only the final two digits are shown, so you can recognise it without the number being reproduced here.
explain.network: Network activity in this record was associated with this country. No exact address or location is stored or shown.
explain.category: A category of personal data that appeared in this record alongside your address.

website.title: Visual graph
website.intro: Your findings grouped by the area they belong to. Select any point to see what it means and what to do about it.
website.subject: Your website
website.subjectExplanation: The domain this report was produced for. Everything below was observed from outside, without logging in.
website.categoryFallback: A group of related findings from this scan.

categoryExplanation.transport: How the connection between a visitor and your site is protected, including certificates and whether HTTPS is enforced.
categoryExplanation.headers: Instructions your server sends with every response that tell the browser what to allow. Most are one-line changes in one place.
categoryExplanation.email_authentication: Whether someone else can send mail that appears to come from your domain. Usually the highest-value area on this page.
categoryExplanation.dns: How your domain name is published and whether those answers can be trusted.
categoryExplanation.exposed_surface: Things reachable from outside that probably should not be, and names registered to be mistaken for yours.
categoryExplanation.software_disclosure: What your responses reveal about the software behind them. Informational rather than a fault.

website.hostsExplanation: Hostnames under this domain that appear in public certificate transparency logs.
website.hostExplanation: A hostname with a publicly logged certificate. If you no longer recognise it, find out what is still running there.
website.lookalikesExplanation: Domains registered by someone to resemble yours. Some will be your own defensive registrations.
website.lookalikeParked: Registered and resolving, but not configured to handle mail.
website.lookalikeMail: Registered and able to send and receive mail, which is the shape of invoice fraud rather than a parked name.
website.lookalikeAction: Confirm this is yours. If it is not, report it to the registrar and warn finance and reception.

website.title: Curious to what we can discover more?
website.body: Our specialized agents and penetration testers with years of experience will perform the pentest.

email.title: This report assessed one identity. AssistSec can assess exposure across your organization and help prioritize remediation.
email.body: One address is a sample. Mapping exposure across your team shows which accounts carry real risk and which are noise, so remediation goes where it counts.

fallback.title: Observation
fallback.observed: We recorded an observation about your public configuration.
fallback.impact: Review this alongside the rest of your findings.
fallback.remediation: Confirm the current setting and correct it if needed.

missing_hsts.title: Strict-Transport-Security is not set
missing_hsts.observed: Responses over HTTPS do not include a Strict-Transport-Security header.
missing_hsts.impact: Without it, a visitor's first request can be downgraded to plain HTTP by an attacker on the same network, and the session can be read or modified before the redirect to HTTPS happens.
missing_hsts.remediation: Send Strict-Transport-Security on HTTPS responses with a max-age of at least six months, once you are confident every subdomain serves HTTPS correctly.

missing_csp.title: No Content-Security-Policy
missing_csp.observed: Responses do not include a Content-Security-Policy header.
missing_csp.impact: A content policy is the control that limits the damage of a cross-site scripting flaw. Without one, any injected script runs with the full privileges of your page.
missing_csp.remediation: Introduce a policy in report-only mode first, review what it would have blocked, then enforce it.

weak_spf.title: SPF does not instruct receivers to reject
weak_spf.observed: The domain publishes an SPF record that ends in a soft-fail rather than a hard-fail.
weak_spf.impact: Receiving mail servers are told that unlisted senders are suspicious but should be accepted anyway, which leaves room to send mail that appears to come from your domain.
weak_spf.remediation: Confirm every legitimate sending service is listed, then move the record to a hard fail.

missing_dmarc.title: No DMARC policy published
missing_dmarc.observed: No DMARC record was found for the domain.
missing_dmarc.impact: DMARC is what tells receiving servers what to do with mail that fails authentication, and what gives you reports on who is sending as you. Without it, spoofed mail using your domain is likely to be delivered.
missing_dmarc.remediation: Publish a DMARC record in monitoring mode, review the reports for a few weeks, then move to quarantine and finally reject.

server_version_disclosed.title: Server software and version are advertised
server_version_disclosed.observed: A response header names the server product and a version number.
server_version_disclosed.impact: This does not make the server vulnerable, and we have not tested whether it is. It does let an attacker match your version against public vulnerability lists without touching you again, which shortens their work.
server_version_disclosed.remediation: Suppress the version from response headers. Treat this as tidying rather than a fix, and patch on its own schedule.

directory_listing.title: A path may expose a directory listing
directory_listing.observed: A request returned a response with the shape of an automatic directory index.
directory_listing.impact: Directory listings can reveal files that were never meant to be linked, such as backups or configuration. This signal is easy to trigger falsely, so treat it as a lead rather than a finding.
directory_listing.remediation: Confirm whether the path really lists files. If it does, disable automatic indexing and check what was reachable.

missing_caa.title: No CAA record restricts certificate issuance
missing_caa.observed: The domain publishes no CAA record.
missing_caa.impact: A CAA record names which certificate authorities may issue for your domain. Without one, any public authority may, which widens the blast radius of a mis-issuance.
missing_caa.remediation: Publish a CAA record listing the authorities you actually use.

no_https.title: The site is not reachable over HTTPS
no_https.observed: A request to https failed to complete, while the domain resolves and answers on plain http.
no_https.impact: Everything a visitor sends, including any login, travels in the clear and can be read or altered by anyone on the network path. Browsers also mark the site as not secure, which most visitors now act on.
no_https.remediation: Obtain a certificate and serve the site over HTTPS. Certificates are free through Let's Encrypt and can be renewed automatically.

no_https_redirect.title: Plain HTTP is served instead of redirecting
no_https_redirect.observed: A request to the http address returned the site rather than redirecting to https.
no_https_redirect.impact: A visitor who types the address, follows an old link, or is steered there by an attacker stays on an unencrypted connection for the whole session. Having HTTPS available does not help if HTTP still works.
no_https_redirect.remediation: Return a permanent redirect from every http URL to its https equivalent, then add Strict-Transport-Security so browsers stop trying http at all.

tls_cert_expired.title: The TLS certificate has expired
tls_cert_expired.observed: The certificate presented on port 443 is past its expiry date.
tls_cert_expired.impact: Browsers show a full-page warning that most visitors will not click through, so the site is effectively down for them. Those who do click through have been taught to ignore exactly the warning that matters.
tls_cert_expired.remediation: Renew the certificate now, and automate renewal so this cannot recur.

tls_cert_expiring.title: The TLS certificate expires soon
tls_cert_expiring.observed: The certificate presented on port 443 expires within two weeks.
tls_cert_expiring.impact: When it lapses the site becomes unreachable for ordinary visitors, and expiries tend to land at inconvenient hours.
tls_cert_expiring.remediation: Renew now rather than at the deadline, and check that automated renewal is actually running.

tls_hostname_mismatch.title: The certificate does not cover this hostname
tls_hostname_mismatch.observed: The certificate presented does not list the hostname that was requested.
tls_hostname_mismatch.impact: Browsers refuse the connection with a warning. Where visitors are used to clicking through it, a genuine interception attempt looks identical to the everyday error.
tls_hostname_mismatch.remediation: Reissue the certificate with the correct names, including every hostname the site is reached by.

tls_chain_untrusted.title: The certificate chain does not validate
tls_chain_untrusted.observed: The chain presented did not verify against the public trust store, though the hostname matches.
tls_chain_untrusted.impact: This is usually an incomplete chain: it works in the browser that cached the intermediate and fails in the one that did not, and in most API clients. The failures are intermittent and hard to attribute.
tls_chain_untrusted.remediation: Serve the full chain, including intermediates, from every server and load balancer that terminates TLS.

tls_legacy_protocol.title: Deprecated TLS versions are still accepted
tls_legacy_protocol.observed: The server completed a handshake when offered only TLS 1.1 or older.
tls_legacy_protocol.impact: These versions have known weaknesses and are no longer accepted by current browsers. Keeping them on serves nobody except an attacker attempting a downgrade, and it fails most compliance baselines.

hsts_short_max_age.title: Strict-Transport-Security expires too quickly
hsts_short_max_age.observed: The HSTS header is present with a max-age below six months.
hsts_short_max_age.impact: The protection lapses for any visitor who has not returned within the window, leaving their next first request downgradeable. A short max-age also fails preload requirements.
hsts_short_max_age.remediation: Raise max-age to at least six months once you are confident every subdomain serves HTTPS correctly.

permissive_csp.title: The Content-Security-Policy permits inline script
permissive_csp.observed: The policy allows 'unsafe-inline' or a wildcard in its script directive.
permissive_csp.impact: A content policy exists to stop injected script from running. Allowing inline script permits precisely that, so the header is present without doing the job it is there for.
permissive_csp.remediation: Move inline script into files, then remove 'unsafe-inline'. Where inline script is unavoidable, use a per-response nonce.

missing_xcto.title: X-Content-Type-Options is not set
missing_xcto.observed: Responses do not include the nosniff directive.
missing_xcto.impact: Browsers may guess the type of a response instead of believing the declared one, so an uploaded file can be interpreted as script. This turns a file upload into a scripting vulnerability.
missing_xcto.remediation: Send X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff on every response.

missing_frame_protection.title: The site can be framed by other origins
missing_frame_protection.observed: Neither X-Frame-Options nor a CSP frame-ancestors directive was present.
missing_frame_protection.impact: Another site can load yours in an invisible frame over its own controls, so a visitor clicking what looks like one thing acts on yours instead. That is enough to trigger state-changing actions.
missing_frame_protection.remediation: Add frame-ancestors to your CSP, naming the origins allowed to frame the site, or 'none' if none are.

missing_referrer_policy.title: No Referrer-Policy is set
missing_referrer_policy.observed: Responses do not include a Referrer-Policy header.
missing_referrer_policy.impact: Full URLs leak to every third party the page loads a resource from. Where a URL contains a token, an identifier or a search term, that is handed out with each request.
missing_referrer_policy.remediation: Send Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin, or something tighter.

permissive_cors.title: Cross-origin requests are allowed from anywhere
permissive_cors.impact: Any website can read responses from this origin. That is harmless for genuinely public data and serious for anything that varies by user.
permissive_cors.remediation: Name the origins that need access instead of using a wildcard, and confirm no authenticated response is served this way.

cookie_not_secure.title: A cookie is set without the Secure flag
cookie_not_secure.observed: At least one Set-Cookie header omitted Secure.
cookie_not_secure.impact: The cookie is sent over plain http as well as https, so a single unencrypted request is enough to disclose it. For a session cookie that is account takeover.
cookie_not_secure.remediation: Add Secure to every cookie. There is no case for omitting it on a site served over HTTPS.

cookie_not_httponly.title: A cookie is readable by JavaScript
cookie_not_httponly.observed: At least one Set-Cookie header omitted HttpOnly.
cookie_not_httponly.impact: Any script running on the page can read the cookie, so a scripting flaw anywhere on the site, including in a third-party tag, becomes a way to steal the session.
cookie_not_httponly.remediation: Add HttpOnly to any cookie that JavaScript does not genuinely need to read.

missing_spf.title: No SPF record is published
missing_spf.observed: The domain publishes no SPF record.
missing_spf.impact: Receiving mail servers have no list of who may send as this domain, so mail forged from it is more likely to be delivered. This is the cheapest impersonation an attacker can attempt against your customers and staff.
missing_spf.remediation: Publish an SPF record listing every legitimate sending service, ending in -all.

spf_allows_all.title: SPF authorises the entire internet
spf_allows_all.impact: This tells receiving servers that any host may send as this domain, which is worse than publishing nothing: it converts a missing policy into an explicit permission to impersonate you.
spf_allows_all.remediation: Replace +all with -all and list only your real sending services.

spf_too_many_lookups.title: SPF exceeds its DNS lookup limit
spf_too_many_lookups.observed: The record contains more than ten mechanisms that each cost a DNS lookup.
spf_too_many_lookups.impact: Past ten lookups the specification requires receivers to treat the record as a permanent error, so SPF stops being evaluated at all. The record looks correct while providing nothing.
spf_too_many_lookups.remediation: Reduce the number of include mechanisms, or flatten them, to stay within ten.

spf_duplicate.title: More than one SPF record is published
spf_duplicate.observed: The domain publishes multiple SPF records.
spf_duplicate.impact: The specification requires receivers to treat this as a permanent error, so neither record is applied and the domain is unprotected despite appearing configured.
spf_duplicate.remediation: Merge them into a single record.

dmarc_policy_none.title: DMARC is published but not enforcing
dmarc_policy_none.impact: Receivers are asked to report on failures and to deliver the mail anyway, so forged mail using this domain still arrives. Monitoring mode is the right place to start and the wrong place to stay.
dmarc_policy_none.remediation: Review your aggregate reports until legitimate senders pass, then move to quarantine and then reject.

dmarc_partial.title: DMARC applies to only part of your mail
dmarc_partial.observed: The record sets a pct value below 100.
dmarc_partial.impact: The policy is applied to a sample, so forged mail continues to be delivered at the remaining percentage. This is a staging step that is easy to forget to finish.
dmarc_partial.remediation: Once reports look clean, remove the pct tag so the policy applies to everything.

dmarc_no_reporting.title: DMARC collects no reports
dmarc_no_reporting.observed: The record has no rua address.
dmarc_no_reporting.impact: Aggregate reports are what tell you who is sending as your domain and what would break if you enforced. Without them you are choosing between staying unenforced and enforcing blind.
dmarc_no_reporting.remediation: Add an rua address and review what arrives before tightening the policy.

missing_mta_sts.title: No MTA-STS policy is published
missing_mta_sts.observed: The domain accepts mail but publishes no MTA-STS record.
missing_mta_sts.impact: Mail delivery between servers falls back to plain text when TLS is unavailable, and an attacker in the network path can force that fallback. MTA-STS is what tells sending servers to refuse rather than downgrade.
missing_mta_sts.remediation: Publish an MTA-STS policy and serve the corresponding policy file, starting in testing mode.

missing_dnssec.title: The zone is not signed with DNSSEC
missing_dnssec.observed: A validating resolver reported the answer as unauthenticated.
missing_dnssec.impact: DNS answers for this domain cannot be verified as genuine, so a resolver that is poisoned or intercepted can point your name at someone else's server with nothing to contradict it.
missing_dnssec.remediation: Enable DNSSEC at your DNS provider and publish the DS record at your registrar.

dangling_cname.title: A DNS record points at a service that no longer exists
dangling_cname.observed: A hostname is aliased to a third-party platform whose target does not resolve.
dangling_cname.impact: On these platforms the name can often be claimed by whoever registers it next, which hands a stranger a hostname under your domain: valid certificates, cookies scoped to it, and your name on their content.
dangling_cname.remediation: Remove the record, or reclaim the service it points at. Treat this as urgent.

exposed_git.title: A .git directory may be readable
exposed_git.observed: A request for /.git/HEAD returned a response with the shape of a Git reference file.
exposed_git.impact: An exposed repository usually yields the full source history, and with it credentials, internal hostnames and the logic of the application. Reconstructing it from a public .git directory is a routine, automated step.
exposed_git.remediation: Confirm the path is reachable, then block it at the web server and rotate anything the repository contains.

exposed_env.title: An environment file may be readable
exposed_env.observed: A request for /.env returned a response with the shape of an environment file.
exposed_env.impact: These files typically hold database passwords, API keys and signing secrets. If it is genuinely readable, treat every credential in it as public.
exposed_env.remediation: Verify the path, remove the file from the web root, and rotate every secret it contains.

exposed_server_status.title: A server status page may be readable
exposed_server_status.observed: A request for /server-status returned a response resembling an Apache status page.
exposed_server_status.impact: The page lists live requests, client addresses and internal paths, which maps the application and its traffic for anyone who asks.
exposed_server_status.remediation: Restrict the handler to localhost or remove it.

large_subdomain_surface.title: A large number of hostnames are publicly certificated
large_subdomain_surface.observed: Certificate Transparency logs list many hostnames under this domain.
large_subdomain_surface.impact: This is information rather than a fault. A wide surface is normal for a large organisation, but each name is something that has to be maintained, and the ones nobody remembers are where forgotten software tends to live.
large_subdomain_surface.remediation: Review the list against what you expect to be running, and decommission anything that should no longer be reachable.

powered_by_disclosed.title: The application framework is advertised
powered_by_disclosed.impact: This narrows an attacker's search before they touch you again. It does not make the site vulnerable, and we have not tested whether it is.
powered_by_disclosed.remediation: Remove the header. Treat it as tidying rather than as a fix.

lookalike_domains_registered.title: Domains resembling yours are registered
lookalike_domains_registered.observed: Common misspellings and alternative suffixes of your domain resolve, meaning someone has registered them.
lookalike_domains_registered.impact: Lookalike domains are the groundwork for phishing that targets your customers and staff, and for invoice fraud in your name. Many are registered defensively by the brand itself, so this needs a look before it needs action.
lookalike_domains_registered.remediation: Check the list against your own registrations. Register the closest few you do not already own, and consider monitoring the rest.

lookalike_domain_with_mail.title: A lookalike domain is configured to send and receive mail
lookalike_domain_with_mail.observed: At least one domain resembling yours publishes mail exchanger records.
lookalike_domain_with_mail.impact: A parked lookalike is a placeholder. One set up for mail is set up to be replied to, which is the shape of invoice fraud and staff impersonation. This is the version of the finding worth acting on.
lookalike_domain_with_mail.remediation: Confirm it is not yours. If it is not, report it to the registrar and the hosting provider, and warn finance and reception that mail from it is not you.

open_directory_index.title: A directory lists its contents to anyone
open_directory_index.observed: A request for a directory returned a server-generated index of the files inside it, rather than a page or a refusal.
open_directory_index.impact: Anyone can read the file names without guessing them. Directory indexes are how forgotten backups, exports and drafts get found, the listing does the searching that an attacker would otherwise have to do by hand.
open_directory_index.remediation: Turn off automatic indexing for that path. In nginx that is `autoindex off`; in Apache it is `Options -Indexes`. Then check what was in there, because the listing has been readable for as long as it has been enabled.

missing_security_txt.title: No security.txt names who to contact
missing_security_txt.observed: Neither /.well-known/security.txt nor /security.txt was published, while other well-known files were.
missing_security_txt.impact: A researcher who finds a flaw has nowhere to send it. In practice those reports go to a sales address, a contact form or a social account, and most of them are never read by anyone who could act.
missing_security_txt.remediation: Publish /.well-known/security.txt with a Contact line and an Expires line, per RFC 9116. It takes one file and turns an unreachable finding into a message that lands.

robots_reveals_paths.title: robots.txt names paths worth hiding
robots_reveals_paths.observed: The site's robots.txt asks crawlers to stay out of directories whose names suggest administration, staging or backups.
robots_reveals_paths.impact: robots.txt is served to anyone who asks, so it is the first file a stranger reads. Listing a path there tells them where to look, and asking a crawler not to index something has never stopped anyone from opening it.
robots_reveals_paths.remediation: Do not rely on robots.txt to hide anything. Put authentication in front of those paths, then remove the entries; if a path must stay unindexed, use a noindex header on the pages themselves.

mixed_content_images.title: An image loads over plain http
mixed_content_images.observed: The page is served over https but references at least one image over http.
mixed_content_images.impact: Anyone on the network path can replace that image or use the unencrypted request to track visitors. Browsers either block it or downgrade the page's security indicator, so the padlock a visitor is looking for stops meaning what they think.
mixed_content_images.remediation: Serve every referenced asset over https, or move the image to a host that supports it. Adding upgrade-insecure-requests to your CSP fixes the symptom while you find them all.

many_third_party_origins.title: Homepage images come from several other companies
many_third_party_origins.observed: Images on the homepage are loaded from three or more hosts outside your domain.
many_third_party_origins.impact: Each one sees the address of every visitor who opens the page, and each one could change what those visitors are shown. This is not a fault, but it is a supplier list most owners have never counted.
many_third_party_origins.remediation: Check that each origin is one you meant to use and can vouch for. Self-host what you can, and pin the rest with subresource integrity where the format allows it.

strong.name: Strong
strong.title: Your public surface looks well kept
strong.body: We found little to correct on the parts of your site reachable without logging in. That is a good sign about how the outside is maintained.

fair.name: Fair
fair.title: Some housekeeping to do
fair.body: We found configuration gaps worth closing. None of them hands an attacker access on its own, but together they make other attacks cheaper.

weak.name: Weak
weak.title: Issues worth acting on
weak.body: We confirmed findings that meaningfully weaken your public position. These are the gaps used as a stepping stone, and most are quick to fix once identified.

poor.name: Poor
poor.title: Act on these findings
poor.body: We confirmed several significant issues on your public surface. We would recommend addressing them soon, and testing the authenticated parts of the application as well.

checks.title: What the free scan looks at

transport.title: The connection, and the certificate behind it
transport.body: We complete a TLS handshake the way a browser would, then read what the server actually presented rather than what it claims to support.

points.0: Certificate expiry, hostname match, and whether the chain is trusted
points.1: Legacy protocol versions still being accepted
points.2: HSTS, and whether plain http quietly serves the site instead of redirecting

email.title: Who is allowed to send mail as you
email.body: SPF, DMARC and MTA-STS are published in your DNS for anyone to read, and they are the records that decide whether a forged invoice from your domain reaches a customer.

points.0: Whether DMARC exists, and whether its policy actually rejects anything
points.1: SPF that ends in a catch-all, or exceeds the ten-lookup limit
points.2: Whether a domain that accepts mail publishes a transport policy

surface.title: Everything carrying your name
surface.body: Certificate Transparency is a public append-only log of every certificate issued since 2018. Reading it maps your hostnames without sending a single packet to you, and it routinely surfaces a host nobody has thought about in years.

points.0: Subdomains found in public certificate logs
points.1: Standard files you publish, and directories a server lists to anyone
points.2: Whether a firewall or a content network sits in front of the origin

impersonation.title: Names built to be misread as yours
impersonation.body: A lookalike domain costs a few euros and is the first move in most invoice fraud. We generate the plausible variants of your name and check which ones somebody has already registered.

points.0: Character swaps, insertions and neighbouring keyboard slips
points.1: Which of those registrations can send and receive mail
points.2: The logos and images a convincing copy of your site would reuse

gate.body: Enter your work details to unlock every finding for this scan.
gate.emailCompany: Use your company email, not a personal one.

agentic.title: What is agentic pentesting?
agentic.intro: The same engagement, carried out by hundreds of specialized agents working under our pentesters.

attack.title: Hundreds of agents, attacking like pentesters
attack.body: Autonomous agents work through your applications, APIs and infrastructure the way a real attacker would, discovering and exploiting weaknesses at machine speed.

prove.title: Every finding is validated before you see it
prove.body: Separate agents re-exploit each candidate finding to confirm it is real. What reaches you is validated, with a working proof of concept, not a pile of unchecked alerts.

report.title: A report the same day
report.body: What used to take weeks now takes hours. Results are validated and exported as the report you need: a management summary, a customer-facing version or the full auditor report.

hero.heading: Monthly recurring pentests.
hero.lede: The initial pentest establishes your baseline. From then on, ARGUS rescans your web applications on the first Monday of every month and shows exactly what changed since the last scan.

points.schedule: A fixed cadence: the first Monday of every month, planned in advance.
points.delta: Every scan compared against the baseline: new, still open, resolved, reappearing.
points.iso: Findings mapped to the ISO 27001 controls they touch, with dates.

model.title: One-off pentests vs monthly pentests
model.p1: A pentest tells you where you stood on the day it ended. The monthly scans keep that answer current, without commissioning a new engagement every time something ships.

pentest.title: The initial pentest
pentest.a: Pentesters and specialized agents test the full scope in depth.
pentest.b: Every finding is validated by an expert before it reaches you.
pentest.c: The result becomes the baseline all later scans measure against.

monthly.title: Every month after
monthly.a: The same scope, rescanned on the first Monday of the month.
monthly.b: We review what changed, and deliver a clear overview to make this understandable.
monthly.c: Fixes that quietly regress come back as reappearing, with history.

lifecycle.title: Multiple finding states to keep track
lifecycle.p1: No archaeology through old PDFs to work out what is new. The comparison is done for you, and each state answers one question.

new.body: Found this scan and absent from every earlier one. Starts its own record.

open.body: Reported before, not fixed yet. Its age is visible, so nothing quietly slips.

resolved.body: No longer reproducible this scan. The fix date stays on the record.

reappearing.body: Fixed once, back again. It reopens with its full history rather than arriving as new.

trend.title: See whether security is improving or slipping
trend.p1: Every scan adds a data point. The trend view plots open findings across months, so a quarter of steady fixes shows up as a falling line and a risky release shows up in the month it happened.

apps.title: Multiple applications, one overview
apps.p1: Scope one application or twenty. Each keeps its own baseline, schedule and history, and the overview adds them up so you can see where risk concentrates.

iso.title: Findings, mapped to ISO 27001 controls
iso.p1: Each finding names the Annex A controls it touches, with dates and evidence attached. When an auditor asks how a control is tested in practice, the answer is a list you open, not a memory.

scope.q: What do the monthly scans cover?
scope.a: The applications agreed in your scope, on the same surface as the baseline pentest. That is what makes results comparable month over month.

timing.q: Why the first Monday of the month?
timing.a: A fixed, predictable date. Your team knows when results land, every scan is exactly a month from the last, and the trend stays honest because the interval never drifts.

certify.q: Does the ISO 27001 mapping make us compliant?
certify.a: No. It shows which controls each finding touches, which supports your audit trail. Compliance and certification remain between you and your auditor.

hero.heading: Instantly retest findings
hero.lede: Request a retest on any finding. The pentester who reported it replays the original attack, keeps your team in the loop on the finding itself, and records the outcome: resolved, or still reproducible.

request.title: Request it from the finding itself
request.p1: Every finding stores its own reproduction steps. When your team ships a fix, the retest is one action on that finding: no scoping call, no new statement of work, no waiting for next month's scan.

thread.title: The conversation lives on the finding
thread.p1: Questions about a fix go to the pentester who wrote the exploit, in a thread attached to the finding. Both sides see the same evidence, and nothing gets lost between a ticket system and a mailbox.

who.a: The pentester who reported the finding wherever possible. Because the original reproduction is stored with the finding, the retest repeats those exact steps either way.

fail.q: What if the fix does not hold?
fail.a: The finding stays open, marked still reproducible, with a note on what still works. Fix again and request another retest; every attempt stays on the record.

cost.q: Is a retest a new engagement?
cost.a: No. You request it from the finding, without a scoping call or a new statement of work. Your agreement with AssistSec sets out how retests are included.

hero.heading: See the pentest while it happens.
hero.lede: Validated findings reach your workspace the moment they are confirmed, ranked with CVSS v4.0. You can watch what ARGUS agents are working on, and when the test completes, you read the report in the same place.

realtime.title: Findings arrive when they are found
realtime.p1: There is no black-box month that ends in a PDF. A finding is published to your workspace the moment a pentester validates it, with reproduction steps and evidence, so remediation can start while the test is still running.

agents.title: Watch the agents work
agents.p1: Our pentesters direct specialized agents, each built for one kind of testing. The activity view shows what is being worked at any moment: which part of your scope, what kind of test, and how far along it is. A finding only reaches your queue after a pentester validates it.

provenance.title: Every finding names the work that produced it
provenance.p1: A finding links back to the agent task and the pentester validation behind it. You can see what was being tested when it surfaced, which is the difference between a result you can act on and an alert you have to interpret.

humans.a: No. Agents carry out testing tasks under a pentester's direction, and a person validates every finding before it reaches your queue.

realtime.q: How quickly do findings reach us?
realtime.a: The moment a pentester validates them. Publication is part of validation, not something that waits for the end of the engagement.

report.q: How is the final report shared?
report.a: In your ARGUS workspace, viewed in the browser over a protected connection. We do not mail it around as an attachment.

hero.heading: ISO 27001 mapping during the pentest
hero.lede: Every finding names the ISO 27001 Annex A controls it touches, with its dates and evidence kept alongside it. When an auditor asks how a control is tested in practice, the answer is a list you open.

points.mapped: Each finding mapped to the Annex A controls it actually speaks to.
points.dated: Found, fixed and verified, each with the date it happened.
points.export: Exportable per control, so an auditor reads it directly.

mapping.title: Every finding names its controls
mapping.p1: A missing security header, an injection flaw and a stale access rule do not belong to the same part of Annex A. ARGUS attaches the controls each finding genuinely touches when the finding is published, so the mapping is made by the people who understand the finding rather than reconstructed later by someone reading a PDF.

coverage.title: Coverage you can show at a glance
coverage.p1: The compliance view rolls the mapping up across your applications, so you can see which technical controls your testing programme speaks to and where the evidence is thin before an auditor finds it for you.

certify.q: Does this make us ISO 27001 certified?
certify.a: No. It gives you dated, technical evidence for the controls a pentest can exercise, which is a real part of your audit trail. Certification is decided by your auditor.

standards.q: Which standard does the mapping follow?
standards.a: ISO 27001 Annex A. Findings name the controls they touch; where a finding speaks to more than one, all of them are attached.

auditor.q: Can our auditor read this directly?
auditor.a: Yes. The evidence per control is exportable, so it can go into your audit file without anyone retyping it out of a report.
